questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_100-->List the old-school and new technologies that can be used for presentations. If you were to give a presentation to a group of baby-boomers who are not tech-savvy, or rather are technophobic, how would you orient your presentation to their needs?

generalfeedback.text:
(Answers may vary.) For presentations, overhead transparencies, chalkboards, whiteboards, and flipcharts would be considered old-school technologies. New technologies could include electronic presentations using Microsoft PowerPoint, Apple Keynote, Google Documents, or a similar software.
Old-school or new, whatever medium you choose, make sure that the audience relates to your message and you are addressing their needs. Even a technophobic audience can be enlivened by a good electronic presentation that is simple and authentic. Carefully consider the colours, background and foreground designs, artwork, fonts, and type styles that you intend to use, as well as aspects such as transitions and builds. Do not cause "death by PowerPoint" by including data-loaded, dull slides. Remember that you are catering to a much older audience who is not comfortable with technology and you do not want to overwhelm them with too much. Focus primarily on the message you are trying to convey and use your presentation merely as a tool to do this.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_101-->You are giving a presentation about "green solutions for organizations," to an audience consisting mostly of members from upper-level management. Based on your knowledge of the benefits of free-form slides versus structured slides, which type of slides will better serve your purpose and why?

generalfeedback.text:
(Answers may vary.) To help convince the audience to make the right decisions when it comes to going green, free-form slides would serve the purpose better. By providing complementary visual and textual data, you can convince the audience more effectively than you would with data-loaded structured slides. By creatively highlighting the key changes in a graph, you can garner audience approval much faster than by just showing multiple slides of tables and interpretations.
Even if the time is limited for your presentation-considering the audience involved-you can include key points in simple slides, with well-designed visuals; hence making sure the audience leaves with the right message. Structured slides are better for routine presentations, not dynamic presentations like the one described here.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_102-->You have to create a presentation for junior high school kids regarding the ill-effects of obesity. Which of these elements would you choose to appeal to your audience and how should they be used: structured or free-form slides? What considerations regarding colour, font, visuals, or background would you keep in mind? Would the backchannel be effective with this group and why?

generalfeedback.text:
(Answers may vary.) Junior high school kids would not respond enthusiastically to structured slides, so visually loaded free-form slides would most likely be the ideal choice. In terms of the other design elements, bright colours would be ideal, the background should be attractive without being distracting, clear and large fonts should be incorporated, and the foreground should include more pictures than typed information. An informative animation would also help garner interest.
The backchannel would likely not be effective with this group because it could distract the audience from the presentation. The presenter could instead encourage live interaction.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_103-->How would the usage of design elements in your presentation differ when presenting to a supportive audience versus a hostile audience?

generalfeedback.text: Student answers may vary but they should incorporate the details of the mindsets that set these audiences apart. Use of fonts, background, colours, and foregrounds can help relay an indirect approach to help diffuse the hostile environment while the same elements used differently can help facilitate the clear, concise, and upbeat presentation that would suit a supportive audience.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_119-->________-any printed materials you give the audience to supplement your talk-should be considered an integral part of your presentation strategy.
<!--RsQ_120-->________ slides help your audience keep track of what you've covered already and what you plan to cover next.
List six ways you can make sure that you are presentation ready. What should you make sure of at least a day or two before you present?

generalfeedback.text:
• Can you present your material naturally, without reading your slides?
  • Could you still make a compelling and complete presentation if you experience an equipment failure and have to proceed without using your slides at all?
  • Is the equipment working, and do you know how to operate it?
  • Is your timing on track?
  • Can you easily pronounce all the words you plan to use?
  • Have you anticipated likely questions and objections?

questiontext.text: List and describe the four types of slides you should include in a formal presentation.

generalfeedback.text:
• Title slide(s). You can make a good first impression with one or two title slides, the equivalent of a report's cover and title page.
  • Agenda and program details. These slides communicate the agenda for your presentation and any additional information the audience might need such as hashtags and Wi-Fi log-in information.
  • Navigation slides. To help your audience follow along, you can use a series of navigation slides based on your outline or agenda. A simple way to do this is to repeat your agenda slide at the beginning of each major section in your presentation, with the upcoming section highlighted in some way.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_123-->Describe why you should provide a presentation handout and what you should include in one.

generalfeedback.text:
Handouts-any printed materials you give the audience to supplement your talk-should be considered an integral part of your presentation strategy. Handouts can include detailed charts and tables, case studies, research results, magazine articles, and anything else that supports the main idea of your presentation. Use handout materials to support the points made in your presentation and to offer the audience additional information on your topic.
Plan your handouts as you develop your presentation so that you use each medium as effectively as possible. Your presentation should paint the big picture, convey and connect major ideas, set the emotional tone, and rouse the audience to action (if that is relevant to your talk). Your handouts can then carry the rest of the information load, providing the supporting details that audience members can consume at their own speed, on their own time. You won't need to worry about stuffing every detail into your slides because you have the more appropriate medium of printed documents to do that.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_124-->Discuss what you should consider when choosing a presentation method.

generalfeedback.text: With all your materials ready, your next step is to decide which method of speaking you wish to use. Speaking from notes (rather than from a written script) is nearly always the most effective and easiest delivery mode. Even if you can memorize your entire speech, your presentation will sound stiff and overly formal because you are "delivering lines," rather than talking to your audience. Worse yet, you might forget your lines. However, memorizing a quotation, an opening statement, or a few concluding remarks can bolster your confidence and strengthen your delivery. Reading your speech is necessary in rare circumstances, such as when delivering legal information, policy statements, or other messages that must be conveyed in an exact manner. However, for all other business presentations, reading is a poor choice because it limits your interaction with the audience and lacks the fresh, dynamic feel of natural talking. Another important decision at this point is preparing the venue where you will speak. Whenever you have the opportunity to arrange the setting, think carefully about the seating for the audience, your position in the room, and the lighting. For instance, for a formal presentation where you're standing on a stage and the audience is in theatre-style seating, it's often a good idea to dim the room lights so people can see the screen more clearly. However, in a less-formal setting where you to want to interact with audience members, you might turn up the room lights and perhaps arrange chairs and tables in a U shape so that you can walk around in the middle of the group.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_125-->Discuss the effective delivery of a presentation and why this is important.

generalfeedback.text:
Use eye contact, posture, gestures, and voice to convey an aura of control and to keep your audience's attention.
As you practise, try to be aware of the nonverbal signals you're transmitting. Regardless of how you feel inside, your effectiveness greatly depends on how you look and sound. Your posture is important in projecting confidence. Stand tall, with your weight on both feet and your shoulders back. Use your hands to emphasize your remarks with appropriate gestures. Meanwhile, vary your facial expressions to make the message more dynamic. Practise speaking in a normal, conversational tone but with enough volume for everyone to hear you and varying your pitch and speaking rate to add emphasis. Use silence instead of meaningless filler words such as um, you know, okay, and like. Silence adds dramatic punch and gives the audience time to think about the message.

<!--RsQ_157-->A line of communication created by people in an audience to connect with others inside or outside the room, with or without the knowledge of the speaker, akin to texting with your classmates or live-blogging during a lecture, is generally known as the ________.
<!--RsQ_158-->________ is a short presentation, usually delivered in 30 seconds to one minute (about the time you spend in a large office elevator).

<!--RsQ_159-->If a presenter has thoroughly prepared for his or her presentation, he or she should be able to effectively handle any kind of question. Is this statement correct? Why or why not? How would dealing with the Q&A of the interested but neutral audience differ from a worried audience?

generalfeedback.text:
Being thoroughly prepared definitely gives the presenter the confidence to handle questions, but he or she may not be able to answer all of them effectively. It helps to be aware of the audience's concerns, keep one's cool while answering difficult questions, and respond diplomatically and honestly. If the presenter does not have an answer to an important question, he or she should offer to provide it after the presentation.
In the case of the interested but neutral audience, address whatever objections that they may have, use the Q&A round to direct their interest into a lively discussion, and encourage dialogue rather than making it a one-man show.
In the case of a worried audience, acknowledge their fears and their feelings and use the direct approach (for good news) and indirect approach (for bad news) appropriately, while answering their queries with honesty.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_160-->Describe ten suggestions for becoming a more confident speaker.

generalfeedback.text: 1. Think positively. Imagine yourself giving a polished and professional presentation. 2. Prepare more material than necessary. Extra knowledge will reduce your anxiety. 3. Rehearse. The more familiar you are with your material, the less nervous you will be. 4. Visualize your success. Use the few minutes before you start to tell yourself that you're ready. 5. Breath. 6. Be ready. Have your first sentence memorized and ready to go. 7. Be comfortable. 8. Take a three-second break. If you find yourself racing, pause, breathe, and perhaps reshuffle your notes. 9. Focus on your message and audience. Think about your subject and your audience. 10. Maintain eye contact with friendly audience members.

questiontext.text: List and explain five tips for embracing the backchannel during a presentation.

generalfeedback.text:
• Integrate social media into the presentation process. For example, you can set up a formal backchannel yourself, create a website for the presentation so that people can access relevant resources during or after the presentation, create an X hashtag that everyone can use when sending tweets, or display the Twitterstream during Q&A so that everyone can see the questions and comments on the backchannel.
  • Monitor and ask for feedback. Using a free service such as X Pro (formerly Tweet-Deck), which organizes tweets by hashtag and other variables, you can monitor in real time what the people in the audience are writing about. To avoid trying to monitor the backchannel while speaking, you can schedule "X breaks," during which you review comments and respond as needed.
  • Review comments afterward to improve your presentation. After a presentation is over, review comments on audience members' X accounts and blogs to see which parts confused them, which parts excited them, and which parts seemed to have little effect (based on few or no comments).
  • Automatically tweet key points from your presentation while you speak. Add-ons for presentation software can send out prewritten tweets as you show specific slides during a presentation. By making your key points readily available, you make it easy for listeners to retweet and comment on your presentation.
  • Establish expectations with the audience. Explain that you welcome audience participation, but to ensure a positive experience for everyone, comments should be civil, relevant, and productive.

questiontext.text: List and explain five tips for giving presentations online.

generalfeedback.text:
• Make sure everyone has time to download and configure any required software. If participants need to do anything to prepare their PCs or mobile devices, send a message well in advance of the presentation with the information they need.
  • Consider sending preview study materials ahead of time. Doing so allows audience members to familiarize themselves with any important background information.
  • Allow plenty of time for everyone to get connected and familiar with the screen they're viewing. Build extra time into your schedule to ensure that everyone is connected and ready to start.
  • Keep your presentation as simple as possible. Break complicated slides down into multiple slides if necessary and keep the direction of your discussion clear so that no one gets lost.
  • Ask for feedback frequently. You won't have as much of the visual feedback that alerts you when audience members are confused, and many online viewers will be reluctant to call attention to themselves by interrupting you to ask for clarification. Setting up a backchannel via X or as part of your online meeting system will help in this regard.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_163-->What is an elevator pitch and when could or should you use one?

generalfeedback.text:
An elevator pitch is a short presentation, usually delivered in 30 seconds to one minute (about the time you spend in a large office elevator). You can use an elevator pitch to sell an idea to investors or clients, to introduce yourself, or to sell your candidacy to an employer.
A good elevator pitch is short, captures attention (with a story, statistics, or humour), is customized for a specific audience (choosing features and benefits for their needs), and is delivered confidently. A typical template could follow this pattern: the problem, your solution, benefits, why choose you over competitors, and a call to action. Use this pattern if you are given only a short time to pitch your product/idea to a potential investor. You can also develop an elevator pitch that introduces yourself. It would briefly tell who you who you are and what you do.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_164-->Discuss how holograms could be used in business.

generalfeedback.text:
If you've ever wanted to be in two places at once, your wish may soon come true. At a recent executive meeting of the global management and technology consulting firm Accenture, attendees included CEO Pierre Nanterme and human resources chief Ellyn Shook.
During the meeting, which took place near Chicago, they chatted with other managers, pitched and listened to ideas, and even shared a few ceremonial fist bumps. Nothing remarkable about that-except that Nanterme was in Paris and Shook was in New York City. Their three-dimensional selves were beamed in as holograms over the company's hyper-advanced information network.
Accenture has long been on the leading edge of communication technology, including the use of advanced telepresence facilities that help its huge workforce stay connected from outposts around the world. As much as Nanterme would like to meet frequently with employees in person, having 375,000 employees spread over 120 countries makes that impossible. In this context, holograms are created by scanning a person or object, vastly oversimplified. Scanning an object with a laser, transmitting the resulting data to a second location, then recreating the person or object as a three-dimensional "figure." The figure is made entirely of light, but today's systems can make the figure look extremely lifelike. Researchers at the University of Tokyo have invented a system that combines holograms with ultrasonic haptic technology that simulates the sensation of touch, making it possible to "touch" a hologram.
Few companies have the resources to do what Accenture can with holograms, and as a technology consulting firm, it has other business reasons to keep pushing the limits of technology. If this use of holograms becomes mainstream, it could change the way geographically dispersed companies communicate. Holograms are already being used in areas such as research and product design, letting people interact with objects that are not physically present.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_045-->Explain how defining your main idea is different from limiting your scope.

generalfeedback.text:
Defining your main idea is the key idea that you want your audience members to walk away with after your presentation. The one-sentence summary should link your subject and purpose to your audience's frame of reference. It would look something like: Address employee concerns regarding a new health-care plan by showing how the plan will reduce costs and improve the quality of their care.
Limiting your scope ensures that you fit in just enough information in the presentation that can be presented in the time provided and that the content meets audience needs and expectations. The longer you speak, the more difficult it is to hold the audience's attention and for listeners to retain key points. The only way to know that your presentation is within the scope is to give it a practice run.

questiontext.text: List and briefly describe the stages that should be included in the presentation outline.

generalfeedback.text:
A presentation outline can be prepared around the following stages:

  1. State your purpose and main idea and then use these elements to guide the rest of your planning.
  2. Organize your major points and subpoints in logical order, expressing each major point as a single, complete sentence.
  3. Identify major points in the body first, then outline the introduction and close.
  4. Identify transitions between major points or sections, then write these transitions in full-sentence form.
  5. Prepare your bibliography or source notes; highlight those sources you want to identify by name during your talk.
  6. Choose a compelling title. Make it brief, action oriented, and focused on what you can do for the audience.

You have been asked to give a presentation at the company summit regarding the new changes in company policy. Your presentation would follow immediately after a very enthusiastic round of ice-breaker games, so you can expect that your audience is going to be quite distracted. How would you arouse audience interest in your presentation?

generalfeedback.text:
Student answers may vary but they could incorporate some of these techniques in their answer.

  1. Unite the audience around a common goal.
  2. Tell a compelling story that illustrates an important and relevant point. If your entire presentation is structured as a story, of course, you'll want to keep the interest high by not giving away the ending yet.
  3. Pass around an example or otherwise appeal to listeners' senses.
  4. Ask a question that will get your audience thinking about your message.
  5. Share an intriguing, unexpected, or shocking detail.
  6. Open with an amusing observation about yourself, the subject matter of the presentation, or the circumstances surrounding the presentation-but make sure any humorous remarks are relevant, appropriate, and not offensive to anyone in the audience.

generalfeedback.text: 1. Catch your audience's attention-start with something they will find important or interesting. 2. Build your credibility-introduce yourself, be confident, explain your credentials to audiences who do not know you. 3. Preview the presentation-help the audience understand the structure and contents of your message.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_072-->After an effective introduction where the audience seemed totally involved, Jessica noticed that she lost her audience quite quickly. People were fidgeting, reading other materials, and a few even left the room. Jessica decided it was the fact that the meeting was held after lunch and people ate too much and got sleepy. Rather than blame the timing (or the buffet table), what advice would you offer Jessica to keep the audience's attention during a presentation?

generalfeedback.text: 1. Relate your subject to your audience's needs-present every point in light of how it will impact the listeners. 2. Anticipate your audience's questions-anticipate listener questions and address them in the body of your speech. 3. Use clear, vivid language-use familiar words, short sentences, and concrete examples. 4. Explain the relationship between your subject and familiar ideas-show how your subject is related to ideas that your listeners already understand. 5. Ask opinions or pause for questions or comments-this lets the audience change from listening to participating.
